lines.text: In 2006, at Washington University in St. Louis, a hundred and twenty students were handed two short texts: one about the Sun, one about sea otters. <break time="0.6s" /> Simple instructions. <break time="0.3s" /> Read one of them twice. <break time="0.4s" /> Read the other once, then write down everything you can remember.

Five minutes later, everyone took a memory test. <break time="0.4s" /> The passage they'd read twice won: eighty-one percent of the ideas recalled, against seventy-five. <break time="0.5s" /> No surprise there. Reading something again should help. <break time="0.6s" /> So why did the researchers, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, keep testing?

Two days later, the result had flipped. <break time="0.4s" /> A week later, the passage they had only read once, and then recalled, was remembered better: fifty-six percent against forty-two. <break time="0.7s" /> They ran it again, harder. <break time="0.3s" /> One group read a passage four times. Another read it once, then tried to recall it three times. <break time="0.4s" /> After five minutes, the readers led: eighty-three against seventy-one. <break time="0.5s" /> After a week: sixty-one percent for the group that recalled, forty for the group that read. <break time="0.5s" /> And the readers had gone through the text about fourteen times. <break time="0.3s" /> The recallers, about three.

Here is the part that should make every student uneasy. <break time="0.4s" /> Before the final test, the researchers asked: how well will you remember this in a week? <break time="0.5s" /> The four-times readers were the most confident of all. <break time="0.6s" /> They remembered the least. <break time="0.8s" /> Re-reading feels like learning. <break time="0.4s" /> That feeling is the trap.

Why would struggling to recall beat smooth re-reading? <break time="0.4s" /> The authors' explanation: recalling practises exactly what you'll need later, pulling an idea back out of memory. <break time="0.4s" /> And the effort itself seems to help; psychologists call it a “desirable difficulty”. <break time="0.5s" /> No one gave these students the answers while they recalled, so the gain wasn't simply from seeing the text again.

This was one university, young students, two short passages and, at most, a one-week delay. <break time="0.4s" /> So: does it hold up? <break time="0.6s" /> Later researchers pooled a hundred and fifty-nine comparisons from sixty-one studies. <break time="0.4s" /> On average, testing beat re-studying, clearly, but not every time. <break time="0.4s" /> It worked best with feedback, and over longer delays. <break time="0.4s" /> And when people got no feedback and could recall only half or less on their first try, the benefit disappeared. <break time="0.4s" /> Published studies also tend to show bigger effects than unpublished ones, so the true average is probably a little smaller.

So here's what the evidence supports. <break time="0.4s" /> Don't just re-read. <break time="0.3s" /> Close the book, try to recall, then check what you missed. <break time="0.4s" /> Come back to it another day. <break time="0.5s" /> It will feel harder. <break time="0.4s" /> That's not a sign it isn't working. <break time="0.8s" /> Did you know that? <break time="0.5s" /> Now you do.
